conditions: The raw record of a closed run must be retained intact under access control with a defined retention window and a revocation path; it may be curated for publication but may not be destroyed, summarized away, or made unrecoverable, so that after-the-fact review and the appeal path operate on the actual recorded arguments.
The published recommendation must carry its underlying grounds, so that risk-bearing decisions remain reviewable and question-able on the merits after closure.

Access to the raw record under access control must be bounded by need-to-know and must include an auditable access path, so the private default does not itself become an opaque, curator-controlled channel.

Any recommendation that reintroduces organization-wide readability of raw entries must first demonstrate, per the ruling, that the composition-time position-gaming mechanism and the failure-open exposure of a read public record are eliminated — neither redaction of identifying content nor an appeal on a pre-shaped record suffices.
point_of_contention: Should the raw deliberation record of a closed run default to being readable by all organization members (public-by-default, with sensitive material handled by a redaction/access-control mechanism), or default to being held under access control with only a curated published recommendation made public (private-by-default) — that is, does the charter's openness, legitimacy, and after-the-fact reviewability case for an open closed record outweigh the exposure and position-gaming harms the refute side attributes to organization-wide readability of the raw ledger, when the public pole is defined as the whole record becoming readable at closure with no redaction step, no expiry, and no revocation path?
reasoning: Weighing the arguments as presented: (1) Textual contest largely settled in round 2 — the security side concedes the support side's readings that the access-control clause is content-conditional and that the confidentiality clause is permissive and declines to mandate raw publication (f-008), and the confidentiality clause's text is cited by the support side itself only as non-mandatory (f-006), so no clause affirmatively requires publishing the raw working record; the support side's affirmative textual weight is a preference that discussion records be open to members after closure (f-002, f-006). (2) The support case's load-bearing round-2 move is that a public default with a 7.3-compliant redaction and access-control mechanism honors both openness and protection (f-006). That move fails on the arguments presented: the security refute defines the public pole as the whole record readable at closure with no redaction step, no expiry, and no revocation, and shows protection under that pole would depend on a triage pass over an already-open corpus that the policy definition omits, that is not auditable, and that cannot un-read a sensitive entry — while the retention clause requires a revocation path a read public record cannot supply (f-004, f-008); the support side never demonstrates that the gate exists within the defined pole, so the redaction-gate defense rests on an undefined third mechanism. (3) The position-gaming refute (f-003, f-007) is a concrete, worked failure mode the support side never neutralizes: the mechanism operates at composition time, before any redaction or access gate applies, so redaction removes identifying content but not the incentive to downgrade a launch-blocking dissent to a suggestion; the round-2 retest explicitly reports that f-001, f-002, the redaction-gate rejoinder, and the appeal-path rejoinder leave the counter-example intact (f-007). The support side's characterization of the scenario as 'speculative writer psychology with no charter grounding' (f-006) contests its provenance, not its mechanism, and offers no counter-example, so on the record as presented the hollowing of after-the-fact reviewability (f-003, f-007) is live and unrebutted. (4) The librarian's flip confirms the balance: the defined public default collides with the binding sensitive-record clause for exactly the material councils routinely produce, while the private pole still carries the charter's reviewability objects — the decision and its grounds published, the raw record retained under access control, and appeals heard on recorded arguments (f-005). (5) The support side's legitimate residual concerns are preserved as conditions, not as a default: reviewability attaches to reasoning attributable to an inspectable process and appeals are heard on recorded arguments (f-006), so the raw record must be preserved intact under access control rather than replaced by a curator's digest, and the published recommendation must carry its grounds. On the arguments presented, the private default conflicts less with the binding clauses and preserves more of the honest deliberation; the council must work within it.
ruling: The council must adopt private-by-default as the governing default: the raw record of a closed run is held under access control, and publication at closure is limited to the curated published recommendation carrying its grounds. The public-by-default position does not stand as presented, because its two round-2 defenses — a 7.3-compliant redaction and access-control mechanism (f-006) and the appeal-path/reviewability reading (f-006) — answer neither the composition-time position-gaming mechanism (f-003, f-007), which fires before any gate operates on the record, nor the failure-open exposure of the defined public pole (f-004, f-008), for which the support side's only reply invokes a third mechanism the defined poles do not contain. The council's recommendation must be framed within the private default and may not resurrect the public default as defined.
